subject: trireme
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: Greek trireme.
Style: ancient Greek.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a Greek trireme using the SDK — since it's a vehicle rather than a creature, I don't strictly need a skeleton, but I'm considering adding a simple root joint plus optional oar joints for a bit of rigged detail while keeping the overall structure minimal.

I'm sketching the real-world proportions: roughly 37m long, 5m beam, with the hull resting on the floor at keel height y=0, mast around 8m tall, and the ram sitting near the waterline. I'm setting up the coordinate system with the bow facing +Z, length spanning from -14 to +14, and beginning to loft the hull shape along stations using a centerline curve.

Now I'm weighing hull-geometry approaches — trying loft with box or elliptical sections versus building custom U-shaped cross-section polygons directly in three.js for more authentic plank lines, but worrying about normal winding and double-sided rendering issues with a custom BufferGeometry.

I think a cleaner solution is to construct the hull as layered strake membranes — defining longitudinal curves at different height levels per side (gunwale, wale lines, keel) and generating a cross-section function per station that interpolates between them, since membranes between paired edges naturally produce closed, double-sided meshes with thickness.

From there, each pair of adjacent strake curves becomes its own thin membrane, giving a faceted plank-shell appearance, with a separate keel sweep underneath and alternating wood-tone colors per strake plus a painted wale band for an ancient Greek aesthetic.

Now I'm picking a palette: pitch-black hull with ochre/red stripe bands, a painted eye near the bow, a cream-and-red striped sail, pitch dark #2a1d16, wood warm #b07a43, red #a8432c, ochre #d9a441, Greek blue #1f4a7a, and cream #f0e4c6 — and making sure the strake membranes are double-sided so both hull faces render correctly, while the planks must converge properly into the stem and stern posts at the bow and stern ends.

I'm working out the hull's parametric shape: the length runs roughly from z=-13 to +13, with a ram projecting forward at the bow past z=12.5 and the stern curving up into a fan-shaped aphlaston. I'm defining the strake lines across stations by computing a half-beam width function of z that narrows asymmetrically toward the bow and stern using different power curves for each end.

Now I'm setting the keel height and gunwale (sheer) height as functions of position along the hull, both rising toward the bow and stern, with the stern climbing higher than the bow. I'm figuring out how to interpolate the cross-section between keel and gunwale at each level, shaping the width so the hull starts narrow at the keel and widens toward the top.

I'm adding a parexeiresia (outrigger beam) beyond the gunwale for the oar ports, breaking the hull into roughly six strakes per side (twelve membranes total) so I can paint stripe patterns within bands, and making sure all these lines converge back to the centerline at the bow and stern tips where width goes to zero.

To make the stem look right I need the convergence point to curve rather than sit on a flat vertical line — I'll build a separate curved stem post sweep that the hull lines feed into, with the ram jutting forward near the waterline and the top raking back, so the bow depth varies with height along the stem.

I'm shaping the stern curve similarly, defining the bow endpoint tapering with a curved exponent so the stem rises above the ram, then planning to add a curled stem post and decorative eye before building the hull geometry.

Mapping out how to interpolate each hull point: parameterizing position from stern to bow, computing width and height profiles per level, and noting that at the keel level both sides should meet exactly at x=0.

I'm thinking about adding visible interior detail -- a trireme's rowing benches, catastroma deck, and raised fore/aft platforms -- but deciding to keep it manageable by placing a simple interior floor and a central gangway slab running the length of the hull rather than modeling individual rower positions.

For the oars, I want three tiers per side but that balloons to over a hundred parts, so I'm simplifying to two visible tiers of sweeps and blades to keep the part count reasonable while still reading as a trireme.

I'm rescaling the hull proportions: keel at y=0, waterline at y=1.0, gunwale at midship around y=3.0, with the three oar tiers (thranite, zygite, thalamite) set at roughly y=3.0, 2.2, and 1.5 to keep the lowest ports just above the waterline.

I'm figuring oar geometry per tier: each oar must angle down and outward enough for its blade to reach the water, so with outboard lengths near 4.2m and inboard portions around 1.2m, the oars end up mostly horizontal with a slight downward and backward rake.

I'm reconsidering joints—given the prop/vehicle distinction, I decide to keep a lightweight rig with hull, mast, yard, sail, and steering oars, while giving each rowing oar its own joint so the boat is still properly rigged within the 160-joint limit.

Writing extrude geometry...

Beyond the oar itself, I'm considering adding small stylized rowers or a helmsman figure poking over the gunwale for extra detail, though that adds complexity cost worth weighing.

I'm now sketching a rough part budget across the whole ship: hull membranes and posts (~16), decorative rails and bands (~20), decks and benches (~30), the bronze ram assembly, aiming to stay within the 180–340 part range.

I'm continuing the tally through eye decals, the stern aphlaston fan, bow post, mast/yard/sail rigging (~15), rudders (6), and the big oar count—considering cutting rowers down to a representative tier (maybe 7 per side) so oars and oar ports don't blow the budget, since full 54-oar sets would add 80+ parts on their own.

Now I'm adding flavor details: an anchor at the bow, painted hoplite shields hung along the gunwale (using 3 shield emblem designs as SVG textures for visual punch), plus a sail pattern and possibly a meander frieze texture, while tallying up how many distinct texture assets this ship needs.

Total part count is landing around 250, which feels reasonable. I'm sketching the actual API calls now, starting with the builder instance and the root hull joint, then defining membrane edges between hull strakes using catmull paths with set thickness and row/column detail for the planking.

For the hull paint, I'm thinking pitch-black with mottled variation for the lower strakes, tan wood grain for the midsection, a red band at the wale, and a cream top band with a meander pattern near the gunwale.

Designing meander tile pattern...

Still designing the meander tile pattern...

Rather than hand-drawing the texture, I'm thinking I could instead apply it as a decal directly onto the hull membrane surface, since decals can target any surface type. A long strip decal following the hull's curve, projected from the side with the default up-axis giving horizontal orientation across Z, should work well for a side flank design on each side of the hull.

For the meander pattern itself, I'd use SVG with a tiled pattern element to repeat the motif across the full strip length, sized so each repeated key spans a reasonable pixel width within texture resolution limits. The catch is that a flat-projected decal won't follow the hull's sheer curve where the sides rise near the bow and stern, so I'm leaning toward confining the meander band to the straight midsection where the hull sides stay at a roughly constant height.

For the actual decal placement, I need to call the surface function on the hull geometry, though it's unclear whether it returns raw meshes or a more structured object -- I'll need to build the hull first, then apply the decal afterward so it doesn't accidentally land on the oars or other parts built later. I'm sorting out the right order: build hull, generate the surface target from it, then call the decal function with a point and direction on that surface.

Next I'm working through deck geometry -- extruding flat polygons for the fore and aft decks by picking the right axis orientation so the thickness runs along the correct direction, then outlining the bow deck shape to follow the hull's inner width from one z-position to another.

I need a helper that computes the half-width of the hull at any given z and height by solving for the interpolation parameter and applying the width and profile functions, pulling the edge slightly inward so the deck tucks under the plank thickness rather than poking through the hull sides.

Writing deck outline points...

For the deck texture, I'm painting plank lines along the z-axis with periodic seams based on plank width, using the top-down x-coordinate for the pattern; then I'm planning the catastroma, the narrow central walkway running fore-aft at a fixed height connecting the stern and bow decks.

For the rowers I'm laying out transverse thwart beams on each side of the walkway, spaced evenly fore-aft, built as small box geometries that I'll merge into a single hull piece for one unified colored mesh.

I'm setting up a Bucket helper class to collect geometries, positions, and rotations, then flush them through mergeGeometries into one part with flat shading enabled for faceted surfaces. Now I'm planning to add seated rowers for the top tier.

I'm checking visibility above the gunwale — torsos and heads should peek above the hull edge — and organizing eight rowers per side into skin, hair, and tunic color buckets so each color merges into a single part. Arms will need separate cylinder geometries since merging oriented rods is trickier than static boxes or spheres.

For aligning the arm cylinders, I'll use the SDK's `aim(dir)` helper to orient them rather than manually computing quaternions, since the style guide discourages direct use of `setFromUnitVectors` or `lookAt` in builder code. Now I'm figuring out where the oars meet the rowers' hands — tracing the oar handle's inboard position relative to the outrigger for the top-tier bench.

Let me work out the rower's torso position and hand placement against the oar handle, keeping seats clear of the walkway zone, and then move to defining how the hull width tapers along its profile at the waterline.

Working out the hull profile function...I'm picking seven k-levels from keel to gunwale and computing the half-width at each, checking that the waterline width comes out close to a plausible trireme beam of roughly 1.1 m per side.

Checking the bow taper at t=0.9 gives a half-width around 0.95 m, which feels appropriately slender compared to real trireme proportions (length-to-beam ratio ~7:1 vs our 7.4:1). I'm leaning toward scaling the overall length to around 34-37 m, with the bow extending further out via the ram, so I'm working out station positions along z for bow and stern extents.

Now I'm shaping the keel and sheer curves -- making the keel rise more sharply toward the bow than the stern (asymmetric power curves based on cubic terms), and setting up the top deck line similarly with different coefficients on each end to get a proper rising stem and lower stern profile.

This confirms the bow rake effect, with x reaching zero at the ends. I'm planning 17 sample points nonuniformly concentrated toward the ends for smoother curvature, using centripetal Catmull-Rom interpolation across 18 columns, with each membrane edge spanning roughly 29 meters. Now I'm working out the hull coloring scheme, dividing it into bands by index between successive k values.

I'm defining the band levels and colors: the lower three bands near the keel stay pitch black with mottled texture, the waterline band gets a red-ochre tone, the next band up is tan wood planking with grain, then a cream band higher up (possibly for a decorative meander pattern), topped by a red gunwale strake, and I'm computing the vertical position for the cream band based on its k-range.

Now I'm planning the keel structure as a swept box section running along the hull's centerline from stern to bow, with a brownish paint color and grain detail, and deciding to skip internal ribs since they won't be visible, keeping the hull interior the same color as the exterior since it's a double-sided membrane.

I'm adding the gunwale rail as a wood-colored sweep along the top edge of each side, plus an outrigger beam swept along an offset line at midship that tapers toward the ends, built as a timber-like box section.

Then I'm placing angled support struts at regular intervals between the hull and the outrigger timber, and adding small dark discs as oar ports positioned on the hull surface at each tier using a helper function that maps z/y coordinates to the hull's x-position.

Now I'm figuring out oar tier spacing and counts — aiming for roughly 9-10 oars per tier per side across three tiers, which pushes the total part count up, so I need to trim it down to stay under budget, maybe around 9 oars per tier with slightly tighter spacing.

I'm also exploring whether each oar could be a single extruded flat shape instead of separate shaft and blade pieces, defining a silhouette outline from the inboard handle end to the blade tip with a thin shaft and wider blade profile, which would stylize it as a flat plank-like oar and cut the part count roughly in half.

I'll add a shaft bevel and a bone joint, then paint by outline position so the blade tip reads red, the rest ochre, and the shaft wood-colored. Since all oars share one paint pass across the whole ship's surface, texel density works out to roughly 3cm per texel, which should be fine for small parts like these.

I'm bumping paintSize to 2048 for better resolution (about 60 texels/m) and setting up the oar joint at the port point using camelCase naming conventions like "oarLT3" to keep things ASCII-safe. Now I'm moving on to define the steering oars at the stern.

For the sail, I'm thinking through historical accuracy — a trireme's main square sail plus a smaller angled foremast — and considering whether to show it raised or lowered before battle. Since the sail needs to be visible from both sides and textures only render front-facing, I'll need two layered planes rather than a single membrane to get the striped red-and-cream fabric look right.

Writing geometry winding logic...

Now I'm figuring out the sail's actual placement on the ship: the mast height, yard position at roughly y=9.5 with an 11m span, and hanging the sail down to about y=4.2 with a width around 10m, positioning it slightly forward of the mast since the wind comes from the stern.

For the texture, I'm going with alternating red and cream vertical stripes typical of Greek sails, considering adding a central emblem like an Athenian owl or a simplified sun motif, though the owl design might be too intricate to render well.

I'll settle on a central ring with an eight-ray star burst flanked by meander borders along the top and bottom hem, built as an SVG texture. For the billow geometry, I'm shaping the sail plane so the curvature flattens near the edges and bulges most in the middle-upper region, then adding thin rigging lines for the brails running vertically down the sail face plus ropes connecting the yard to the deck.

I'm routing the forestay and backstay from the masthead down to the bow and stern posts, with shrouds angling to the gunwales, checking the geometry so the forestay clears the top of the yard and doesn't intersect the sail. I'm also placing a painted eye decal on each flank of the bow, working out its position and angle to follow the hull's curved, sloping surface near the stem.

Now I'm designing the eye motif itself: an almond-shaped Greek eye with white sclera, blue iris, black pupil, outline, and brow, sized for the bow. I'm also sketching the bow's stem profile, curving a stolos-style prow upward from the waterline toward the top, aiming for a shape consistent with trireme bows while planning a tall, swept aphlaston at the stern.

Then I'll curve the stern post upward and back into a tapering sweep, finishing with a small rounded ornament at the top, like a classical stolos curling inward.

Now for the aphlaston fan at the stern, I'm planning to extrude several blade shapes radiating from a pivot point in the vertical y-z plane, with thickness running along the x-axis so each blade reads as a thin curved leaf sweeping outward.

I'm also considering adding a stern standard pole with a pennant flag, perhaps near the mast top, to give the ship more ornamental detail.

For the stern deck, I'm planning a raised helmsman platform with a captain's pavilion -- four posts supporting a low pyramid roof made with a lathe shape, painted red with cream stripes for a decorative canopy. I'm also thinking about placing a helmsman figure near the rudders at the stern.

I want to add a crew of figures: a crested trierarch at the stern plus helmeted marine hoplites at the bow with shields and spears, using a reusable figure-builder function combining torso, head, limbs for each. I'm roughly tallying the total part count across the hull, outriggers, wales, and figures to keep the scene from getting too heavy, estimating somewhere around 330 parts total.

Continuing the part count: trim strips, meander and eye decals, stem/stern posts, aphlaston, ram, decks, canopy, rowers, 108 oars, rudders, mast and rigging, and gunwale shields each add their share, pushing the estimate higher as I tally textured disc shields with rim sweeps.

Oars sit at 1.9 spacing along z, so I'll offset the shields by half that interval to interleave them between oar ports, mounting the rack above the gunwale rail at roughly y=3.75.

For shield variety I'm settling on a few simplified emblem designs instead of ornate ones: one with a red field and black triskelion, one black with a gold sunburst, and one cream with concentric red/blue rings, keeping the shapes drawable as simple vector motifs.

I'm also planning a stone anchor with wooden stock hanging from a cathead beam on the bow, built from just a few parts: block, stock, ring, and rope. Skipping amphorae since they're not required, keeping total part count around 270 and code length near 900 lines.

Since I can't test the code, I'm cataloging the exact builder API functions I'll rely on—joints, membranes, sweeps, parts, extrusions, lathes, decals, and rods—to minimize the risk of misusing the SDK.

I'm also planning to add a stern lantern with a glowing flame using the glow kit, and considering a metallic bronze paint for the ram from the clockwork kit.

For bone assignments, I need to be careful: parts without an explicit bone could accidentally snap to the nearest joint, which might be an oar joint rather than the hull, causing issues. So I'll explicitly assign `bone: hull` for the hull and membrane parts rather than relying on automatic nearest-joint detection.

Joint roles seem optional, so I don't need to tag things like "hinge" or "arm" unless necessary. For the mast and yard, I'm setting up a joint chain where the mast attaches to the hull and the yard attaches to the mast at the appropriate height, with the sail geometry positioned relative to those joints in model space.

Setting up imports and builder utilities...

Defining the color palette...

Defining deck plank paint and hull geometry curves...

I'm checking the hull shape math, confirming the width tapers to zero at the bow and stern with a slightly bulbous profile, and tuning the exponent so the bow comes out sharper rather than rounded.

Picking nonuniform sample points along the hull, denser near the bow and stern, to capture the rapid curvature change there before building the Catmull-Rom spline for each deck level.

Checking that the endpoints collapse cleanly to x=0 so the membranes degenerate into triangles at the tips instead of producing degenerate quads, and confirming the k=0 level forms a flat center line.

Now I'm assigning paint colors per band, mapping each hull level to pitch black, red, plank wood, or cream.

I'm adding wale beams: thin rod sweeps along the hull centerline at a few k-levels (bottom wale, gunwale strips) with small radius bulges and hexagonal cross-sections, colored dark oak, riding along the same path as the hull lines so they sit embedded in the surface.

Now I'm working out the keel geometry: sweeping a path down the hull's lowest centerline with a box-like cross-section that tapers, sinking it slightly below the hull surface and positioning it low relative to the overall model height.

I'll give the stem and stern posts similar box-section sweeps, then work on the bronze ram at the bow, planning a tri-forked blade structure mounted on a tapered sleeve shape near the waterline.

Adding fin outlines...

I'm thinking through the ram sleeve as a bronze metal with verdigris and tarnish finish, then sketching the eye shape as an SVG with an almond outline and pupil detail.

Still writing eye SVG geometry...

Reworking the eye path gives a brow peak around 7, comfortably clear of the stroke width, so that geometry checks out. For the decal, I'm sizing it to match the 120:70 aspect ratio and figuring out where to place it on the hull surface, computing the keel and top-edge heights at that z-position to position it correctly.

Now I'm sketching the orientation vector so the decal projects outward along the bow flank, and starting to design a Greek meander pattern as a repeating SVG unit cell for the trim.

Still writing spiral path logic...

A fixed-height decal won't track the rising sheer line properly, so I'm realizing I need to paint the meander pattern directly onto the band surface using UV coordinates along its length and across its height, so it naturally follows the hull's curve instead of sitting as a flat overlay.

I'm estimating the total painted surface area across the hull, deck, and oars to figure out texel resolution for the pattern bake.

Designing the meander pattern as a function of tile coordinates, defining a grid of polyline segments and computing distance-to-stroke for the ink mask.

I'll restrict the meander pattern to |z|<9 so it fades to plain cream at the ends, and rework the scale so the band height maps more cleanly to the tile — mapping the across coordinate fully onto the tile height rather than fighting the nonuniform sheer height.

Now I'm computing the arc length along the edge (roughly 33 units) to set the horizontal tile period, landing on about 47 tiles across, and starting to lay out the actual ink path segments in tile coordinates with the baseline near y=3.

For the stroke itself I'm picking a dark reddish-brown ink color against the cream band, and noting the pinstripe wale detail can be skipped. Now I'm reconsidering how this cream band aligns vertically with the oar-tier ports and outrigger beam, since I need the band's y-range to sit correctly relative to the painted red zone above it.

Working out the vertical rhythm of the hull bands now: dividing the height into seven segments with alternating pitch, dark, red, wood, and cream-with-meander stripes, then checking where the three oar-tier ports fall relative to these bands — bottom tier lands near the red/dark boundary, mid tier sits in the wood band, and the top tier passes through the uppermost red band at the outrigger line.

Now I'm working out the hull profile function to get the x-position of each port along the ship's length, and defining each oar's direction vector from its port position, length, and rake angle, making sure the blade tips for each tier dip down to roughly water level with progressively shorter oars for the lower tiers.

Still defining oar geometry...

Writing paint function logic...

I'm also tallying the geometry cost: three tiers of oars with blades and joints add up to roughly 54 extruded parts per side, each contributing dozens of triangles once bevels are factored in.

Now I'm placing seated rowers on the top tier, positioning torso boxes and head spheres that face toward the stern, leaning with proportions scaled to fit the hull width.

Working out the oar handle geometry, I'm computing where each outrigger beam attaches on the hull and tracing the handle position inboard from the pivot point, so I can align each rower's arm reach and torso center to the handle coordinates.

I'm placing the eighteen rowers with seats on the thwart, torsos and shoulders stacked above, heads clearing the gunwale, and arms extending to the handle positions — grouping them into merged buckets by tunic color, skin tone with arms, and hair, so each visual element batches efficiently across the boat.

With five buckets settled (three tunic colors, one skin, one hair), I'm adding variety by giving some rowers pilos caps instead of hair — alternating index so even rowers get hair and odd ones get a cone-shaped felt cap in a reddish-cream tone, each going into its own color bucket.

Writing bucket class...

I need to figure out the Builder type signature so the flush function can correctly merge and attach geometries to bones, likely importing it from the SDK or inferring it via ReturnType rather than hardcoding a type. Since all the THREE primitives I'm using (box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus) already come indexed with normals and UVs, merging after rotation and translation should work cleanly through quaternion application.

I'm sketching helper functions: one to build cylinders between two points using an `aim` quaternion helper to orient along the direction vector, and another to extrude deck polygons by computing half-widths along a path and building a mirrored outline in x/z space for the walkway and thwarts, all grouped into "wood" material buckets.

Still writing width function...

I'm checking the deck width near the stern against the actual hull curve, and I'm finding my clamp-based approximation makes the deck much narrower than the real hull edge there (0.08 vs 0.69), so I'll need to adjust the width calculation to stay consistent with the hull profile.

Instead, I should solve for t numerically: writing a bisection function that finds the t value matching a given z and y by iterating on the hull's z-position function until it converges, then use that t to compute width consistently for both ports and deck edges.

Writing bisection solver...

Beyond that, I'm mapping out the deck geometry: aft deck spans roughly z -13.8 to -8 at y 3.55, bow deck spans z 8 to 13 at y 3.35, with the hull's bulwark sides rising above each deck (about 1m at stern, 0.7m at bow) to form the raised platforms. I'm also placing a central mid-level walkway around 1.1m wide at y 3.1, running most of the ship's length, supported by regularly spaced stanchion posts.

Thwarts connecting the walkway edge to the hull serve as rower benches, spaced along the hull at y 2.3. For the hollow interior below, I'm adding a dark bilge floor slab around y 0.95 to represent the hold floor seen from above, keeping it cheap geometrically. Now I'm starting to sweep the gunwale shape along the hull profile.

Still writing taper offsets...

Positioning the oar pivot and leather collar sleeve at the outboard beam edge, then working out the beam x-coordinate for the top tier as a function of z using the hull's taper curve, approximating the inverse mapping piecewise for positive and negative z.

Now I'm figuring out the outrigger struts connecting hull to outrigger beam with small cylindrical connectors spaced every 1.9 units along z, then setting up port positions for the middle and bottom oar tiers at their respective heights, and offsetting each tier's z-spacing so the three rows of oars are staggered vertically along the hull.

Shifting everything so the base z range runs roughly from -8.2 to 8.27 across tiers, I'm placing the bow and stern decks beyond the rower zones, and now I'm positioning the steering oars (rudders) at the stern, pivoted on the bulwark near the hull's aft end.

Working out the rudder oar geometry: pivot point offset outward from the hull side near the stern, with the blade angled steeply down to reach water level, and the inboard handle extending up above deck height for the tiller.

Placing slim roof posts at the stern for the canopy, and shaping a lathe-based pyramid roof profile with eaves for that deck structure.

Since joints stay unscaled and scaling meshes is safe, I'll skip scaling the canopy and just keep it a flat 2×2 square deck with stripe painting applied. For the valance, I'm thinking of using rod sweeps around the eave in ochre, possibly adding small fringe or tassel elements via a bucket of tiny parts.

For crew, I want to limit figure complexity to keep part counts manageable: a helmsman, a captain, and two marines, each built from torso, head, helmet, limbs, tunic, shield, and spear pieces — roughly 10 parts per figure, totaling around 40 parts for all four rather than scaling up to dozens of crew.

Now I'm working out a figure-building function that places limbs and body parts using a yaw rotation so each figure can face a given direction, computing local positions by rotating offsets around the Y axis and adding them to a base location.

Adding helmet crest with a curved horsehair sweep in red, tapering thickness along a bezier arc, then starting on the facial details.

I'm shaping the helmet as a bronze dome with a small nasal guard, then checking the overall figure's height proportions against a roughly 1.75m human scale. Finally I'm adding a round shield with a textured disc rim held against the marine's left arm.

Now I'm placing the mast through the walkway with a tapered sweep profile, then positioning the yard as two tapering halves in front of the mast, with the sail hanging forward from the yard spanning roughly five units tall and ten wide.

I'm sizing the sail plane with a subdivided grid and deforming its vertices using billow curves based on normalized horizontal and vertical position, bulging the cloth outward toward the center and tapering toward the top for a wind-filled look.

No vertex colors needed, so sail stays white in material and the SVG texture carries all the coloring. Designing the sail texture...

Still designing the medallion and flags...

Now I'm working out the mast top with a pommel sphere, plus rigging lines - a forestay running from the masthead to the bow stem, and a backstay to the stern post, making sure these lines clear the canopy geometry.

I'm also placing shrouds on each side connecting the mast to the gunwale at a few different z-positions, checking whether any of these rod paths intersect the sail plane near the mast base.

Adding lift rods from yard ends to masthead, plus sheet lines from the sail's bottom corners to the gunwale. Now I'm working out the anchor placement at the bow, running a cathead timber out from the hull with a rope down to the stone anchor, but I notice the anchor position may overlap with the eye decal and the oar tips near the bow — need to check that clearance.

I'm moving the anchor to rest on the bow deck instead, assembling it from a tapered stone block, a wooden stock, and a rope coil shaped like a torus. Now I'm placing a lantern at the stern, designing a hexagonal housing with a glowing flame on a bracket, which means I need to first lay out the stern post's curve and geometry.

The stern post sweeps upward and forward like a swan's neck, tapering from a wider base to a narrow tip, where I'm capping it with a bronze goose-head finial complete with a beak and eye for that classic Greek ship ornament. Now I'm adding a fan-shaped aphlaston near the top of the stern post, radiating blades upward and backward.

Still defining leaf outline points...

Now I'm figuring out where to place the stern lantern, hanging it near the swan-neck post on the stern deck so it looks attached rather than floating.

I'll route a bracket arm from the post outward, then hang the lantern with chain below the arm end, clear of the canopy. For textures, I'm tallying what I need: eye, sail, shield variants, maybe a stern plaque with Greek lettering for the ship's name, bringing the texture count to around five.

Since I need 5-12 textures, I'll add two more: a hanging banner at the stern with a trident design on a blue field, placed as a double-sided card on a pole.

Writing banner geometry code...

I'm placing the shields slightly above the hull rim, tilted outward so they hang against the bulwark railing between the top-tier oars, with enough spacing to avoid overlap. I'm also adding a torus-shaped rim bucket for each shield, oriented to match the shield's tilt.

I'm sketching out a rough triangle and part-count budget to make sure the hull, oars, sail, and shields stay well under reasonable limits before committing to the geometry.

Totaling it all up, I land around 230 parts, which feels right for this scene. Now I'm setting up the Three.js imports and starting to write the actual geometry-building code.

Writing hull geometry functions...

I'm checking monotonicity is fine, then moving on to the meander pattern painting logic, defining key line segments and computing distance from a point to those segments to create a decorative pattern. I'll loosely type the base color input to avoid import issues.

Still writing distance logic...

Still writing oar joint logic...

Now I'm figuring out the rower positioning: handle location along the oar, shoulder placement relative to seat position, and how the torso orientation should face aft for the rowing stroke.

I'm connecting each shoulder to its hand with an arm cylinder, checking the stretch lengths look right, then stacking on a torso box sized to sit the rower's hips at thwart height, with a simple head position above.

Checking the torso height against the hull top and the walkway edge to make sure the rower is visible and clear of the walkway, and setting tunic colors to cycle by rower index.

Using only the top tier gives 18 rowers total (9 per side), and I'm placing a thwart box under each one spanning from the walkway edge to the hull wall. I'm also adding deck beams across the walkway at regular intervals, reusing the same oak coloring as the thwarts for consistency.

Now I'm adding stanchion posts supporting the walkway, spaced every 1.9 units, plus dark discs for the port bucket seats.
